items.simple_meaning: To change words from one language into another language.
items.explanation: When you translate, you keep the meaning the same but say or write it in a different language. In India, many people translate between Hindi, English and their home language every day.
items.example_sentence: Meera helped her grandmother translate the English school notice into Tamil.
items.real_world_usage: Can you translate this Marathi song into English for me?
items.spelling_guidance: Think of it as 'trans' (across) + 'late'; the noun 'translation' drops the final 'e' before adding '-ion'.
items.learning_objective: Learners will use 'translate' to describe changing words or ideas from one language into another.
items.illustration_brief: A girl sitting beside her grandmother at a table, pointing at a printed notice, with two speech bubbles showing different script shapes (no readable words) linked by an arrow.

items.simple_meaning: To share ideas, information or feelings with others.
items.explanation: We communicate by speaking, writing, using gestures or even drawing pictures. Good communication helps people understand each other and work well together.
items.example_sentence: Our cricket team learnt to communicate with hand signals so the fielders knew where to stand.
items.real_world_usage: I communicate with my cousin in Pune by writing letters during the holidays.
items.learning_objective: Learners will use 'communicate' to talk about different ways people share ideas and feelings.
items.illustration_brief: Children on a cricket field using hand signals to each other, with small arrows showing the message passing from one child to another.

items.simple_meaning: To take air into your body and let it out again.
items.explanation: You breathe in air through your nose or mouth, and your lungs take in oxygen your body needs. Then you breathe out the used air.
items.example_sentence: After running in the school race, Arjun sat under the neem tree to breathe slowly and rest.
items.real_world_usage: Our yoga teacher tells us to breathe in deeply and breathe out slowly.
items.spelling_guidance: 'Breathe' (verb) ends with an 'e'; 'breath' (noun) does not. You take a breath, but you breathe.
items.learning_objective: Learners will use 'breathe' correctly and tell it apart from the noun 'breath'.
items.illustration_brief: A child sitting cross-legged on a mat in a garden, eyes calm, with soft curved lines showing air flowing in and out of the nose.

items.simple_meaning: To become healthy again after being ill or hurt.
items.explanation: When you recover, your body slowly gets better after a fever, cold or injury. Rest, good food and medicine from a doctor can help you recover.
items.example_sentence: Priya stayed home with a fever during the monsoon, but she will recover in time for the school trip.
items.real_world_usage: I drank warm soup and rested so I could recover from my cold.
items.spelling_guidance: Split it into re + cover; the 'y' in 'recovery' makes the noun.
items.learning_objective: Learners will use 'recover' to describe getting better after an illness or injury.
items.illustration_brief: A child resting in bed by a window with rain outside, a glass of water and a bowl of soup on a small table, looking relaxed and comfortable.

items.simple_meaning: To remove something, such as a word or a file, from a computer or device.
items.explanation: When you delete something on a computer, you take it away so it no longer appears. It is a good idea to check carefully before you delete anything important.
items.example_sentence: Kabir had to delete an extra photo from his project slides before showing them in class.
items.real_world_usage: I will delete this wrong spelling and type the word again.
items.learning_objective: Learners will use 'delete' to describe removing items on a computer or device.
items.illustration_brief: A child at a school computer lab pressing a key, with a simple picture icon on the screen fading into a small bin symbol.

items.simple_meaning: Feeling pleased because you got what you wanted or needed.
items.explanation: You feel satisfied when something turns out well, like finishing work you are proud of. It is a calm, happy feeling of being content.
items.example_sentence: After decorating the rangoli for Diwali, Ananya stepped back and felt satisfied with the bright pattern.
items.real_world_usage: I am satisfied with my science model because I worked hard on it.
items.spelling_guidance: The 'y' in 'satisfy' changes to 'i' before adding '-ed': satisfy → satisfied.
items.learning_objective: Learners will use 'satisfied' to describe feeling pleased with a result or effort.
items.illustration_brief: A child kneeling beside a colourful finished rangoli at a doorstep, smiling calmly, with small diyas glowing around it.

items.simple_meaning: Difficult in a way that tests your skill or effort.
items.explanation: Something challenging is hard but possible if you try your best. Challenging tasks help us learn and grow stronger in our skills.
items.example_sentence: The maths puzzle in today's class was challenging, but our group solved it together.
items.real_world_usage: Learning to bowl a spin ball is challenging, but I keep practising.
items.spelling_guidance: Remember 'll' in the middle: cha-LL-enging, and drop the 'e' of 'challenge' before adding '-ing'.
items.learning_objective: Learners will use 'challenging' to describe tasks that are difficult but achievable with effort.
items.illustration_brief: A small group of students around a desk working on a puzzle sheet with shapes and numbers, looking focused and determined.

items.simple_meaning: To stop being angry with someone who has done something wrong.
items.explanation: When you forgive someone, you let go of hurt feelings and give them another chance. Forgiving helps friendships stay strong.
items.example_sentence: Rohan said sorry for breaking my kite before Makar Sankranti, so I decided to forgive him.
items.real_world_usage: It's okay, I forgive you for forgetting to bring my book.
items.spelling_guidance: Think 'for' + 'give'; the past tense is irregular: forgave, forgiven.
items.learning_objective: Learners will use 'forgive' to talk about letting go of anger and repairing friendships.
items.illustration_brief: Two children on a rooftop, one holding a torn kite and the other offering a new one, both smiling as they shake hands.

items.simple_meaning: To achieve what you were trying to do.
items.explanation: You succeed when your hard work helps you reach your goal. Sometimes you need to try many times before you succeed.
items.example_sentence: After weeks of practice, Fatima finally managed to succeed in playing the whole tune on her harmonium.
items.real_world_usage: If we plan well, our team will succeed in the science quiz.
items.learning_objective: Learners will use 'succeed' and 'succeed in' to describe reaching a goal through effort.
items.illustration_brief: A child playing a harmonium in a cosy living room with a proud family member clapping nearby and music note shapes floating in the air.

items.simple_meaning: To suddenly understand or become aware of something.
items.explanation: When you realise something, a fact becomes clear in your mind. You might realise you forgot something or understand the answer to a problem.
items.example_sentence: Halfway to school, Dev began to realise he had left his tiffin box on the kitchen table.
items.real_world_usage: I just realise now that the answer was in the first paragraph!
items.spelling_guidance: In Indian/British English it is spelt with 's': realise, realised, realisation.
items.learning_objective: Learners will use 'realise' to describe the moment of understanding or becoming aware of something.
items.illustration_brief: A boy with a school bag stopping on a path, hand on his forehead, with a thought bubble showing a tiffin box on a kitchen table.
